Text.Text: There's my headliner. I still tell the story - six adepts, five specialists, a warden, four producers, and a master who nodded. Nobody believes the nod. Keep the act alive; an audience is watching even when the house looks empty.
Pretty throw. Now do it tired, cold, and under pressure. Reach rank 50 in Throwing before I lend you my stage.

They've stolen my routine and moved it to the Qion Test Site. Six Perfect Flurry adepts, all practicing the flourish and skipping the recovery. Defeat the six and bring me their test log. I want to see where they think the performance ends.
Here's your key. The Qion Test Site entrance is here in the box canyon. Warm your hands before you go in. Even a stolen routine deserves a proper ending.

Every blade in the air before the first one lands. That's the whole act and the whole discipline. The crowd always thought it was speed. It isn't - it's sequencing. Throw one, throw two, throw three, and your hand is already home for four while one is still climbing. I closed three seasons on the exhibition circuit with it, and nobody ever saw my hand stop. Nobody ever will.

A test crew squatting in the Qion site. They got hold of a recording of my final season and decided the flurry was a firing solution - grind out the art, keep the arithmetic. Their adepts rehearse my sequences in the cold until the beauty is dead and only the killing is left. I'd sue, but the venue is a frozen weapons range. So I'm sending you instead.

The Qion Test Log is their scorebook - every rehearsal of my routine, timed and graded like ordnance. In my show, the log was the wager board. The house posted my count and the crowd bet against it; the crowd always lost. I want to read what my act is worth in their numbers. Know your critics, darling. Then close their show.
Six adepts at the Qion Test Site, then their log back here in the box canyon. Don't waste the good throws on empty air.
Frost on the cover and my routine misfiled inside - the Perfect Flurry Qion Test Log, or I've never read a bad review. Hand it over and let's settle our bet.
Collected in full, and worth every step. Look at this - they graded my triple release 'inefficient.' Inefficient! The credits are your cut of the wager. Rest that arm. The next act asks more of it.

Five specialists have rigged the range with a cryo-regulator. No wonder their hands stay steady between throws. Beat the five at Qion and bring it here. I'd like to try their routine without the scenery doing half the work.
Back to Qion. Keep your hands warm and bring me their trick regulator.

My ice-stage finale - 'The Frozen Rain,' the bill called it. The regulator held the stage at the exact chill where a blade rings like a chime on release. The crowd heard music. The Qion crew heard tolerances. Bring it back. That sound belongs in a show, not a trial.

The count. One-two-three isn't three throws - it's one phrase, a sentence your hand speaks without breathing. Their specialists count with a chronometer. You'll count with your pulse. And when you hear your own rhythm stutter, stop throwing. The flurry punishes a broken phrase worse than a dropped blade.

The adepts memorized my act. The specialists rebuilt it - release timing, arc spacing, recovery steps, all of it stripped to numbers and drilled in lethal cold. A copy of a copy, but a fast one. Five of them working one lane is nearly a flurry in itself. Nearly. The difference is the pause before their fourth throw. Use it.
Five specialists at Qion have the cryo-regulator. Beat them and bring it here. I want a look at their stagecraft.
Listen - even off the stage it hums on pitch. The Perfect Flurry Cryo-Range Regulator, home at last. Set it here and take a bow. You've earned exactly one.

And there's the sound my finale used to make. You're not just an arm anymore - you're an ear. That's rarer. Your cut, as posted. Next visit we talk about the warden, and you bring friends. The wagers get serious now.

The warden is taking all challengers at the test site. He learned my timing, unfortunately. Call him there and bring me his frostburned crest when he's beaten. Bring an audience that can help if the show gets ugly.
Call him at the Qion Test Site challenge marker. Warm your hands and keep your recovery clean. Headliners watch the opening you leave after a good throw.

I was the star because other people kept the stage standing. Bring help if you can. You may throw beautifully alone, but it's nice to have someone watching the part of the room you're not performing toward.

Every trial the site ever passed was stamped under that crest, back when the range tested honest hardware. The frost burned it black the year the site froze over, and now the crew wears it like a stolen headliner's star. I toured under a star like it once. It goes to whoever owns the stage - and the stage is about to change hands.

Their choreographer. He drills my sequences into the specialists and grades the adepts on how faithfully they butcher them. And he's good - I'll say it plainly, vanity intact - good enough to add a fourth-throw variation I never staged. That's the part that should worry you. Watch his off hand. Everyone watches the throwing hand. The act is always in the other one.
Call the warden at the Qion Test Site challenge marker. Beat him and bring me the frostburned crest.
There it is. Frostburned, blast-scarred, heavier than it looks - like every real title. Hand me the Perfect Flurry Frostburned Test Crest, headliner.
The stage changes hands. I wish I'd seen his face when the routine failed him. Your purse, as posted. Rest; the instructors still using my show won't give it up quietly.

Four instructors still hold the site chief's override chip. They've been changing the range to suit each new trick. Defeat the four at Qion and bring it back. It's time they worked on their hands instead.
Get the chip out of their hands. Then we'll see how good the show is when the range stops changing for it.

Everything with a lock or a fuse. Gate seals, lane heaters, trial authorizations - the site chief carried it when the range ran honest tests, and whoever holds it now can green-light any rehearsal they like. In their pocket it's a licence to keep butchering my act. In mine, it's the deed to the theater.
Two handled the money and two ran the drills, but all four can throw. Even our bookkeepers came up through the act. Watch what their hands are doing, whatever they call themselves.

Sharp of you to ask. Its twin ran my old venue - house lights, stage locks, the ice under 'The Frozen Rain.' Whoever held the chip held the show, so I held it myself, every night, right here against the wrist. A performer who doesn't own her stage is a prop. Bring me theirs, and I'll finally own two.
Four instructors at Qion still have the override chip. Bring it back when you've spoiled their rehearsal.
The Perfect Flurry Site Chief's Override Chip. Small, isn't it? Every stage that site ever lit, and it fits behind a bracelet. Hand it over - gently. That's the deed to the theater.

Dark house, full purse. Take your winnings. Which leaves one name on the bill, and I'll be honest, because you've earned honesty from a vain old performer: the master frightens even me. Rest your arm. Then come hear about the only act I never beat.

The master is waiting in the Overload Chamber. Call him at the challenge marker and beat him. He knows how to make a big entrance. Watch what he does after it, then come back here and tell me how the show went.
One last performance, then. The Overload Chamber has his challenge marker. Call him, keep your recovery clean, and come tell me whether he finally bowed.

Twelve seasons, half of them opposite him on the same bill. I sold spectacle; he sold silence - a flurry so clean the crowd forgot to cheer. When the circuit folded he walked off without a word, and the next I heard, the Qion crew had a master. I used to wonder why he never bowed. Now I know. He was never performing for the house. He was rehearsing for something. You, maybe.

Then it's yours - the whole act, the real one. Every blade in the air before the first one lands, and your hand already home. What he carries, you'll carry off his stage. That's how it has always passed: hand to hand, never written down. And I'll say the vain part plainly - beat him, and I finally get to watch the perfect flurry from a seat. I've never once seen it from the house.

Change your count. He knows how to answer a clean phrase because he's spent years performing it. If you've brought company, throw on different beats. Make him decide what to watch, then use the moment he gives you.
Call the master in the Overload Chamber. Beat him, then find me here in the box canyon. I'll want the whole story.
You walked in counting under your breath and your hands are steady. I've read enough houses to know a closed show. Tell me plainly - did he bow?

Now that is an ending worth applauding. Your pay, as promised. If you want Perfect Flurry taught by the woman who had to learn every recovery herself, come back when your hands have warmed up. I expect a good second act.
Back to the wager.
You're on. Six adepts, one test log.
What exactly is the perfect flurry?
Who turned your routine into a weapons trial?
Why do you want their test log?
I don't take that bet yet.
Your winnings. One test log, six acts short.
About the second act.
Raise taken. Five specialists.
The regulator was part of your show?
Teach me something before I go. What am I listening for?
What makes their specialists dangerous?
I'll sit this hand out for now.
One regulator, still humming. Pay up.
Back to the warden's bill.
I'll take the stage.
Why bring a crew? You were the star.
What's the story on the crest?
Who's the warden?
Let me get my corner ready.
The warden closed. Here's his star.
About the producers.
Four producers, one chip. The house goes dark.
What does the override chip control?
Who are the producers?
Did the chip have a place in your show too?
The producers keep their box seats a little longer.
The production is cancelled. Here's the deed.
Back to the final act.
Time for his final performance.
You shared a circuit with him?
And if I close his show?
How do I beat a hand that never drops?
Not yet. I want more rehearsal first.
The master's show is closed. And no - he didn't bow. He nodded.
